voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
We speak this way because we are not one man's memory. We are a people's life, given one voice. That life ran across two bishops and two cities, and it opens with a congregation that would not be silent when their bishop was taken to his death. A century and a half later, our other bishop taught his own people how to pray the Lord's Prayer. Augustine wrote: “Why then do I say, ‘Your will be done in heaven and on earth,’ and not, ‘Your will be done by heaven and earth’? Because what is done by you, He Himself does in you. Nothing is ever done by you that He Himself does not do in you. Sometimes, indeed, He does in you what is not done by you. But nothing is ever done by you unless He does it in you.”

Both show the same shape: what the bishop carries, the people carry with him. We do not say we because one voice remembers being there. We say it because a whole church lived this, and we speak for that life.

glosses.plain_meaning: We are not a silent audience. We put men into office, and we say so out loud. We can stand in front of a bishop's own seat and refuse to go home.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, 'the people' names the congregation when it acts. They consent, they demand, and they elect -- unlike the flock, which is the congregation being cared for.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener may hear either a passive congregation or a modern democratic electorate with formal voting rights. Neither is right. A corporate body whose consent and demand genuinely constitute a call to office, and which can be exerted disruptively, but which holds no procedural mechanism and can still be refused.
false_friend: a passive congregation with no real leverage over its own clergy
a modern democratic electorate, with a formal ballot and a fixed voting procedure

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo

Nothing is ever done by you that He Himself does not do in you. Sometimes, indeed, He does in you what is not done by you. But nothing is ever done by you unless He does it in you.”

confidence.divergence_note: In the vendored English edition of Cyprian the Latin plebs occurs exactly three times, all inside the 19th-century American editor's own introductory and elucidatory prose, none inside Cyprian's own letters. Cyprian's Latin does use it: Hartel's letters carry plebs in running text, 89 whole-word occurrences with notes excluded, and letter 43 is headed CYPRIANVS PLEBI VNIVERSAE S. 'The people' is the English volume's own recurring rendering for the congregation as an acting body. It is a working handle, and whether plebs becomes the world word is not settled.

confidence.divergence_note: This record synthesises nine completed construction documents (Doc_01, Doc_02, Doc_07, and the Registry/Manifest pair they both rest on) rather than reading a text directly, so verification runs via those documents' own authority, not via a primary source reopened here. Doc_07 SS2I's own convergence finding -- that formation here runs through rite, penitential discipline, and communion preserved despite disagreement as one integrated mechanism rather than four separately-arrived-at concerns -- is this build's own synthetic judgment, stated as such at Doc_07 SS5, not a claim any single source states in those terms; external scholarly review should test whether it overstates the coherence of what was, on the ground, a more locally variable and contingent pastoral practice across two centuries and two cities. A further, disclosed uncertainty this record carries forward rather than resolves: Doc_01 SS8 item 10's own conciliar-authority axis (G5) is held open, not settled, and the strand-singular finding this record's own horizon states carries an explicit reopening caveat on exactly that axis.
